title: What Is TEFL and Who Is It For?
brief: Introduce TEFL as a field by drawing on the module's description of the materials as designed for 'both new and experienced EFL teachers and teacher trainers.' Explain that EFL (English as a Foreign Language) is the context in which English is taught in countries where it is not the dominant language, using the module's framing of classrooms 'from around the world.' Clarify that the field serves a wide range of practitioners—from those just starting out to seasoned trainers—and that entering it means joining a global community of educators who observe, evaluate, adapt, and act on their teaching. Keep the tone welcoming and broad; avoid any methodology detail.

title: The Range of Learners: From Very Young Children to Adults
brief: Use the module's four-part learner classification to map out who English language learners are: Very Young Learners (ages 5–6), Young Learners (ages 6–12), Teens (secondary level), and Young Adults and Adults (post-secondary). For each group, draw on the module's brief descriptions—for example, the very young learner classroom where students choose learning stations and a science lesson is delivered, and the Costa Rica EFL classroom of beginner 5–6-year-olds using puppets, songs, and games. Emphasise that learner age shapes everything from classroom arrangement to activity type, without going into methodology. This section should help new teachers appreciate the breadth of possible student populations they may encounter.

title: Contexts and Settings: Where English Is Taught
brief: Draw on the module's examples of varied classroom settings to show new teachers that TEFL happens across a wide range of contexts. Highlight the contrasting settings mentioned in the module: a bilingual English-Spanish classroom in the United States and an EFL classroom in Costa Rica, both at the primary level. Use the module's framing of videos featuring 'a variety of English language classroom settings from around the world' to convey that public school classrooms, bilingual programmes, and foreign-language contexts each present different conditions. Note that classroom environments vary enormously—the source contrasts a 'large and well-equipped' classroom with the implicit reality that many teachers work in less-resourced settings—and that teachers must adapt to their local context. Do not discuss online teaching beyond what the module supports.

title: What Differs Across Contexts: Age, Level, and Environment
brief: Explore how teaching conditions change depending on the learner group and setting, using concrete contrasts from the module. Draw on the module's notes that very young learners require transition management, learner autonomy routines, and movement-based activities such as Total Physical Response, songs, and games, while post-secondary learners engage with different structures entirely. Use the module's observation that managing transitions 'can be difficult, especially when working with very young learners' and that classroom size and resources vary, requiring teachers to adapt ideas to their local context. Also draw on the lesson plan template's fields—number of students, level, institution, lesson length—to illustrate the variables a teacher must account for. Avoid prescribing specific methods; focus on raising awareness of difference.

title: What the Job Actually Involves: Core Professional Practices
brief: Give new teachers a realistic picture of what TEFL work looks like day to day, drawn entirely from the module. Use the module's list of pedagogical skills developed through the materials—classroom management, language teaching techniques, encouraging critical and creative thinking, lesson observation skills, and adapting activities and lesson planning—as the backbone of this section. Describe the 'observe, evaluate, adapt, act' cycle the module presents as central to professional practice, and note that reflection is built into the job: the module explicitly encourages teachers to keep 'notes or an informal reflective log' of what went well and what to change. Reference the lesson plan template's evaluation questions (what did students learn, what was most or least successful, what changes will you make) to show that planning and self-assessment are routine professional tasks.

title: Learning from Other Classrooms: Observation as a Professional Tool
brief: Introduce the idea that watching and reflecting on other teachers' classrooms is a recognised part of professional life in TEFL, using the module's 'observation to action' framework. Explain that the module describes observation as an experience that can 'help teachers better understand how they approach their own students, curricula, and classroom routines,' and that the process moves through defined steps: activating prior knowledge, pre-viewing, viewing with focus, and then planning action. Note that the module encourages teachers to compare observed practices to their own classes and then 'adopt or adapt' ideas to fit local needs—a principle that applies whether a new teacher is watching a colleague, a recorded lesson, or reflecting on their own class. Close by reinforcing that this reflective, outward-looking habit is part of what it means to be a TEFL professional from the very start.
